etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English *cowardly (adjective) and cowardly (adverb), equivalent to coward +‎ -ly. Displaced native Old English earg.

definitions.definition: Showing cowardice; lacking in courage; weakly fearful.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene vii]:
quote.text: The cowardly rascals that ran from the battle.

quote.citation: 1780, Edmund Burke, speech at The Guildhall, in Bristol
quote.text: The cowardly rashness of those who dare not look danger in the face.

definitions.definition: (archaic) In the manner of a coward, cowardlily.

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act II, scene v:
quote.text: We will not ſteale vpon him cowardly,But giue him warning and more warriours.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, translated by John Florio, The Essayes […], book I, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC, page 48:
quote.text: I love to follow them, but not so cowardly, as my life remaine thereby in subjection.

quote.citation: 1828, John Paul, A Refutation of Arianism‎[1], page 20:
quote.text: […]  men who cowardly and hypocritically subscribe orthodox creeds, whilst they teach a different kind of doctrine!
